title: Tensor orbit-closure intersection in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\)
formal:
Is the tensor orbit-closure intersection language \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\) defined below in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\)? Equivalently, does it have both polynomially bounded certificates for yes-instances and a two-message public-coin Arthur–Merlin protocol for no-instances, with the completeness and soundness conditions below?

A valid input specifies positive integers \(n,m\) and two triples \(X=(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})\) and \(Y=(Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3})\) of \(nm\)-by-\(nm\) matrices with coefficients in \(\mathbb Q(i)\), given by their full lists of entries. On the ambient complex vector space
\[
\mathcal X_{n,m}=\bigl(\mathbb C^{nm\times nm}\bigr)^{\oplus3},
\]
the group \(G_{n,m}=\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb C)\) acts by
\[
(A,B)\cdot(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})=
\bigl((A\otimes B)X_{1}(A\otimes B)^{-1},
      (A\otimes B)X_{2}(A\otimes B)^{-1},
      (A\otimes B)X_{3}(A\otimes B)^{-1}\bigr).
\]
The input belongs to \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\) exactly when
\[
\overline{G_{n,m}\cdot X}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}
\cap
\overline{G_{n,m}\cdot Y}^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}
\ne\varnothing.
\]
Invalid encodings do not belong to the language. Both dimensions and all coefficient bit lengths are unbounded parts of the input; the number of matrices in each triple is fixed at three. Prove membership in both complexity classes, or prove that membership in their intersection fails. This is the tensor-class specialization of the explicit certificate question in the source, selected from its broader exact-complexity discussion.

source_formulation.text: Outlook and open problems It remains an open question to determine the exact complexity of OCI problems.
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 8

why: Tensor orbit-closure intersection captures when allowed basis changes can bring two algebraic objects to a common limit. Locating this class within NP and coAM would determine whether both sides of a broad family of geometric equivalence problems admit short, efficiently checkable evidence, connecting invariant theory with the certificate structure familiar from graph isomorphism.
status_note: Question I.11 of the FOCS 2025 source explicitly raises NP∩coAM membership, and the latest listed revision dated 2 December 2025 retains it. The target deliberately specializes that question to the TOCI-complete double-conjugation problem over Gaussian-rational input. Primary-source reading and bounded subsequent checks through 16 September 2026 found no resolution of this membership assertion; the checked 2026 algorithms concern fixed-dimension special-linear actions or average-case compact-group actions. This is a bounded source-open assessment, not an exhaustive proof of present openness. The narrowing is an explicit editorial choice rather than an asserted equivalent reformulation of the broader source question.

progress.text: Lysikov and Walter’s Theorem I.1 proves completeness of the three-component double-conjugation problem for \(\mathrm{TOCI}\), and Theorem I.5 establishes graph-isomorphism hardness. Question I.11 explicitly asks whether orbit-closure intersection can be placed in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\), alongside other unresolved class comparisons.

The latest listed arXiv revision of Lysikov and Walter retains Question I.11 and the same field, encoding and completeness framework. It does not provide the required general certificate and interactive-protocol characterization.

Cai and Young’s Corollary 40 gives a \(\mathrm{TOCI}\)-complete Holant-indistinguishability problem with two ternary contravariant components and one binary covariant component. This adds a complete representative, rather than an \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\) upper bound.

Doğan, Maar, Oliveira and Qiao prove that orbit-closure intersection for \(\mathrm{SL}_{n}(\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{SL}_{n}(\mathbb C)\times\mathrm{SL}_{m}(\mathbb C)\) acting on \(\mathbb C^{n}\otimes\mathbb C^{n}\otimes\mathbb C^{m}\), with \(m\) fixed, is in \(\mathrm{coRP}\). The algorithm takes Gaussian-rational inputs and polynomial bit time for each fixed \(m\); its group action and fixed-dimension regime differ from the complete problem used here.

sentences: The input consists of two triples of Gaussian-rational matrices, with two dimensions allowed to grow.
Each triple is acted on by simultaneous conjugation using a Kronecker product of two invertible complex matrices, and the decision asks whether the two orbit closures intersect.
The selected source subquestion asks whether yes-instances have short NP certificates and no-instances have a polynomial-time public-coin Arthur–Merlin protocol.
This is a complete representative of the tensor orbit-closure class, which includes graph isomorphism and tensor-network indistinguishability problems.
A complete Lean proof must establish both certificate guarantees for all inputs or refute their conjunction, while the broader original exact-complexity question remains distinct.

definitions:
For a positive integer \(a\), write \([a]=\{1,\ldots,a\}\). Identify matrix rows and columns with \([n]\times[m]\) in lexicographic order. The Kronecker product is specified by
\[
(A\otimes B)_{(u,v),(u',v')}=A_{u,u'}B_{v,v'}.
\]
The same pair \((A,B)\) acts on all three matrices in a triple. Here \(\mathrm{GL}_{a}(\mathbb C)\) is the group of all invertible \(a\)-by-\(a\) complex matrices; its elements are not restricted to rational entries, determinant one, or unitary matrices. The inverse in the action is the ordinary matrix inverse, not a conjugate transpose. The input matrices need not be Hermitian, positive, normalized or invertible. This matrix representation identifies \(\mathcal X_{n,m}\) with
\[
\bigl(V\otimes V^{*}\otimes W\otimes W^{*}\bigr)^{\oplus3},
\qquad V=\mathbb C^{n},\quad W=\mathbb C^{m},
\]
where the stars denote complex-linear dual spaces, on which the group acts by the inverse dual action.

For a subset \(S\subseteq\mathcal X_{n,m}\), its Zariski closure is
\[
\overline S^{\,\mathrm{Zar}}
=\{z\in\mathcal X_{n,m}:\ \forall p\in\mathbb C[\mathcal X_{n,m}],
\ ((\forall s\in S,\ p(s)=0)\Longrightarrow p(z)=0)\},
\]
where \(\mathbb C[\mathcal X_{n,m}]\) is the ring of polynomials with complex coefficients in the \(3n^{2}m^{2}\) matrix-entry coordinates. The orbit is \(G_{n,m}\cdot X=\{g\cdot X:g\in G_{n,m}\}\). In this setting the Zariski and Euclidean closures of each orbit coincide. The decision predicate concerns intersection of the two closures, not equality of the original orbits, containment of one orbit closure in the other, or a positive-distance approximation promise. A point in the intersection may have arbitrary complex coordinates and is not supplied with the input.

The coefficient field for the finite input is fixed as \(\mathbb Q(i)=\{a+ib:a,b\in\mathbb Q\}\), embedded in \(\mathbb C\) with \(i^{2}=-1\). Write each coefficient uniquely as \(p/q+i\,r/s\), where \(p,r\in\mathbb Z\), \(q,s\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), \(\gcd(|p|,q)=\gcd(|r|,s)=1\). Thus a zero real or imaginary part has denominator one. An unsigned integer is its usual binary expansion with no leading zeros, with zero written 0. A signed integer is a sign symbol, \(+\) or \(-\), followed by the unsigned expansion of its absolute value; the sign of zero is always \(+\).

To encode an instance, form a list of tokens: first \(1^{n}\), then \(1^{m}\), then the tokens \(p,q,r,s\) for every coefficient of \(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3},Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3}\), in that order and with each matrix listed in row order. Numerators use the signed format and denominators the unsigned format. Place the separator \(\#\) between consecutive tokens and no separator at either end. Turn this five-symbol string into binary using
\[
0\mapsto000,\quad1\mapsto001,\quad\#\mapsto010,
\quad+\mapsto011,\quad-\mapsto100.
\]
All other binary strings are invalid, including strings with the wrong number of entries, invalid dimensions, noncanonical fractions or unused three-bit codes. Let \(t=|z|\) be the complete bit length of an input string \(z\). Both unary dimension tokens and every sign, numerator and denominator bit count toward \(t\). This fixes an exact language on \(\{0,1\}^{*}\); it does not use a real-arithmetic oracle or a succinct tensor representation.

A deterministic verifier is one multitape Turing machine with a finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes, and the indicated read-only input tapes. A transition reads and writes at most one symbol per tape and moves each head by at most one cell, and counts as one step. Inputs start between end markers; the machine returns a single accept/reject bit. There is no advice, oracle, uncharged preprocessing, or unit-cost operation on arbitrarily long integers or complex numbers. The machines, polynomial length bounds and time bounds are fixed before the input \(z\), and all running-time guarantees are worst-case bounds. Every polynomial length or time function below has fixed nonnegative integer coefficients; time bounds are positive. Such bounds may be enlarged by polynomial padding without changing the classes.

The assertion \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\in\mathrm{NP}\) means that there exist a deterministic verifier \(V_{N}\), a polynomial certificate-length function \(a:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), and a polynomial time bound \(T_{N}\), such that, for every input string \(z\) of length \(t\), the verifier halts within \(T_{N}(t)\) steps on every auxiliary string \(w\in\{0,1\}^{a(t)}\), and
\[
z\in L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{a(t)},\ V_{N}(z,w)=1.
\]
Thus every yes-instance has some accepting certificate, and no certificate is accepted on a no-instance.

The assertion \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\in\mathrm{coAM}\) means that its complement has the following Arthur–Merlin protocol. There exist a deterministic verifier \(V_{A}\), polynomial functions \(b,c:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), and a polynomial time bound \(T_{A}\). On input \(z\) of length \(t\), Arthur samples \(r\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{b(t)}\) using independent fair bits and sends the entire string to Merlin. After seeing \(z,r\), Merlin returns an arbitrary string \(w\in\{0,1\}^{c(t)}\), and Arthur accepts exactly when \(V_{A}(z,r,w)=1\). Merlin has no computational restriction. The verifier must halt within \(T_{A}(t)\) steps on every such \(z,r,w\). Define the maximum acceptance probability
\[
\alpha(z)=2^{-b(t)}
\left|\left\{r\in\{0,1\}^{b(t)}:
\exists w\in\{0,1\}^{c(t)},\ V_{A}(z,r,w)=1\right\}\right|.
\]
The required completeness and soundness inequalities are
\[
z\notin L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\Longrightarrow\alpha(z)\ge\frac{2}{3},
\qquad
z\in L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\Longrightarrow\alpha(z)\le\frac{1}{3}.
\]
The existential response is inside the probability over Arthur’s message because Merlin sees that message. There is no input distribution and no restriction to generic tensors. The randomness belongs only to Arthur; an auxiliary witness need not encode an algebraic transformation or a common limit.

For the class-level wording, a polynomial-time many-one reduction from a language \(A\) to a language \(B\) is a single deterministic polynomial-time map \(f\) on binary strings such that \(z\in A\) if and only if \(f(z)\in B\). The source proves that the double-conjugation problem above is complete for the tensor orbit-closure intersection class \(\mathrm{TOCI}\), with the input coefficient field fixed to \(\mathbb Q(i)\). Thus \(\mathrm{TOCI}\) can equivalently be defined here as all languages polynomial-time many-one reducible to \(L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\). Since \(\mathrm{NP}\) and \(\mathrm{coAM}\) are closed under these reductions, the target is equivalent to \(\mathrm{TOCI}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\) for this fixed coefficient field.
answer_criterion:
An accepted answer is a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of
\[
L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\in\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}
\]
or of its negation for the exact input language, complex group action and bit model specified above.

A positive answer supplies the two uniform verifier machines and their polynomial bounds, proves the deterministic certificate equivalence for every binary input, and proves the public-coin protocol’s completeness and soundness inequalities for every binary input and every allowed prover response. The relevant existential choices of machines and polynomials must precede the universal quantifier over the input. Certificates and messages can be arbitrary binary strings of the specified lengths; no additional semantic form is required.

A negative answer proves
\[
L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\notin\mathrm{NP}\quad\lor\quad
L_{\mathrm{OCI}}\notin\mathrm{coAM}.
\]
Here each nonmembership assertion is the negation of the full verifier-and-polynomial existence statement in the definitions, so it excludes every eligible verifier with every polynomial choice, rather than just a particular certificate format or algorithm. A conditional nonmembership result under an unproved assumption does not settle this unconditional question. Membership in just one of the two classes, a special dimension regime, an average-case result, or a protocol with unspecified bit lengths and running time is insufficient. This is a class-membership proposition, so no additive numerical tolerance applies.

context_blocks.text: The source asks broadly for the exact complexity of orbit-closure intersection, while this card deliberately selects its explicit \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coAM}\) subquestion for the tensor class over Gaussian-rational input.

Triples of matrices under the displayed double-conjugation action form a complete representative for this class, so the fixed number of components retains the general tensor-class membership question.
Lysikov and Walter reduce graph isomorphism to tensor orbit-closure intersection, showing that the problem already includes a central equivalence-testing task.
Cai and Young identify a further complete problem through indistinguishability of tensor-network contractions, connecting the same class to counting-problem equivalence.

The 2026 randomized polynomial-time result for a special-linear tensor action with one fixed dimension treats a different family and does not establish the proposed membership for the complete double-conjugation problem.

Model audit: identify V⊗V*⊗W⊗W* with matrices on V⊗W, giving simultaneous conjugation by A⊗B on exactly three components. Right factors act through inverse duals, not complex conjugation. Both n and m vary, and inputs are arbitrary Gaussian-rational matrices with no closed-orbit, genericity, invertibility or positivity promise. The closure is taken over C even though the input is finite. The source’s unary dimension encoding is retained and explicit reduced fractions with a fixed binary alphabet coding count all bits. The polynomial-class question is unaffected by such ordinary polynomially interconvertible dense encodings.

Verifier audit: NP uses one existential polynomial-length certificate and exact deterministic verification; coAM is AM for the complement, with Arthur’s public uniformly random string first and an arbitrary bounded-length Merlin response afterward. Thus the quantified event is Pr_r[exists w: V_A(z,r,w)=1], not exists w Pr_r. Completeness is at least 2/3 on strings outside the OCI language; soundness is at most 1/3 on strings inside it. All messages, clocks and machines are uniformly polynomial in total input bit length and fixed before the input. Invalid encodings are outside the language. A refutation means the full language is outside NP or outside coAM, not a counterexample to one intended algebraic certificate.
